a1_answer:
NOVELTY STATEMENT — Standard practice tracks equivalent series resistance (ESR) and capacitance as direct indicators of supercapacitor health. My observable is the electrolyte volume fraction, inferred from the temperature dependence of ESR, which directly probes the electrolyte depletion mechanism rather than just its electrical consequence. This departure connects to failure physics because electrolyte dry-out reduces ion mobility, which manifests as a non-linear increase in ESR with temperature that deviates from the expected Arrhenius relationship.

PHYSICS CHECK — The governing relation is the Nernst-Einstein equation: σ = (nq²λ)/(kT), where σ is conductivity, n is ion concentration, q is charge, λ is ion mobility, k is Boltzmann constant, and T is temperature. As electrolyte volume fraction decreases, n and λ decrease non-linearly, causing σ to drop more steeply than expected. For a typical organic electrolyte, conductivity decreases by ~2%/°C; a 15% deviation from this rate indicates electrolyte depletion below the 10% capacitance loss threshold.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL — Components: 1) Existing temperature sensors (module surface and ambient), 2) Existing current/voltage sensors for ESR measurement, 3) Onboard processing unit capable of real-time calculation. Procedure: Measure ESR at multiple operating temperatures during normal cycling. Calculate the temperature coefficient of ESR (d(ESR)/dT) and compare against the baseline value from new modules. No new hardware required—uses existing sensors with updated firmware. Development needed: Algorithm to extract temperature coefficient of ESR from operational data.

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY) — Installability: Same (no additional sensors). Operability: Same (uses existing measurements). Maintenance: Same (no additional maintenance points). Cost class: Same (software update only). The approach maintains parity with standard practice while providing earlier detection of electrolyte dry-out through a physics-based indicator rather than waiting for catastrophic ESR increase.

EXECUTABLE TEST — Protocol: Subject 10 modules to 65°C ambient cycling between 0V and 2.7V at 1Hz for 1000 hours while monitoring ESR at 25°C, 40°C, and 55°C. Calculate temperature coefficient of ESR weekly. Instruments: Environmental chamber, data acquisition system, existing vehicle sensors. Pass/fail: Pass if temperature coefficient deviation remains <15% over test duration; fail if deviation reaches 15% before 1000 hours. Kill criterion: Immediate termination if any module shows >10% capacitance loss or ESR increase >50% from baseline. Duration: 1000 hours or until failure criterion met.
